units.text: Start with the two Availability Zones on the left, where separate public, application, and data subnets allocate different amounts of address space.
The spare ranges beside them reserve capacity for future growth, rather than consuming the whole VPC allocation on the first deployment.
On the right, compare two hundred fifty one usable addresses in a slash twenty four subnet with one thousand nineteen in a slash twenty two subnet.
Return to the full layout and size for network interfaces, pods, and future zones, because changing an existing subnet size requires replacement and migration.
Follow the central hierarchy from the top level private pool to separate regional pools, then down to the nonoverlapping VPC allocations.
The two VPCs beneath the US East pool receive different slash twenty blocks within the same larger regional allocation.
On the right, allocation rules guide size and tags, utilization monitoring exposes problems, and authorized pool sharing uses AWS Resource Access Manager.
With the whole diagram visible, centralize allocation before expanding across accounts, while planning a separate migration for any overlap that already exists.
Compare the two upper VPCs: both use the same address range, preventing direct peering and creating conflicting destinations for shared routing.
The lower diagram shows the intended outcome, with Account B moved to a different range so the networks have distinct route destinations.
Follow the numbered sequence on the right: inventory dependencies, reserve a nonoverlapping range, migrate workloads, then validate routes, security, and rollback.
Return to the full slide and its caveats: adding another range does not remove the old overlap, while PrivateLink can expose a particular service without providing full network connectivity.
